record.paper_title: Open Problems in Communication and Computation
record.original_question: What would a comprehensive theory of computational complexity look like?

evidence.quote: What is a comprehensive theory of computational complexity?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Formulate a comprehensive mathematical theory of computational complexity. Concretely, propose a unified framework that:

1. Defines a general notion of a computational problem and a model of computation (e.g., Turing machines, Boolean circuits, arithmetic circuits, communication protocols, query/decision trees, quantum circuits, distributed/parallel models), together with associated resource measures (time, space, circuit size and depth, communication, randomness, queries, energy, nonuniformity, etc.).

2. Specifies complexity classes as sets of problems solvable within prescribed bounds on these resources, and defines reductions and completeness in a model-independent way.

3. Provides general principles or axioms (in the spirit of Blum's axioms or abstract complexity) from which the main known separations, hierarchies (time, space, nondeterministic), simulations, and trade-offs follow uniformly, and which permit proofs of unconditional lower bounds for explicit problems.

4. Yields, as theorems within the framework, resolutions of the central open separation questions: P vs NP, NP vs coNP, P vs PSPACE, NL vs P, BPP vs P, BQP vs classical classes, and the existence of one-way functions.

5. Explains and unifies the known barriers (relativization, natural proofs, algebrization) to proving such separations, and identifies which proof techniques can or cannot circumvent them.

The problem is: construct such a theory, prove its internal consistency and explanatory power, and use it to settle at least one of the major separation problems listed above, or prove that no such theory satisfying the stated criteria can exist.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is broad and foundational. The central separation problems it asks any such theory to resolve (e.g., P vs NP) remain open as of 2026, and no widely accepted "comprehensive theory of computational complexity" in the stated sense exists; known barrier results (relativization, natural proofs, algebrization) show that current techniques are insufficient.

status_evidence.title: P versus NP problem
status_evidence.snippet: The P vs NP problem remains one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems and is unresolved.
status_evidence.claim: Central separation problems demanded by any comprehensive theory are still open.

status_evidence.title: Natural Proofs (Razborov–Rudich)
status_evidence.snippet: Natural proofs constitute a known barrier to proving circuit lower bounds.
status_evidence.claim: Barriers to a unified lower-bound theory remain in force.
